q: Which statement about the developing kidney is FALSE?
o: Neonatal sodium balance is a key task
GFR reaches adult levels at birth
e: The metanephros forms the mature nephrons; the pronephros involutes fully and the mesonephric duct forms parts of the urinary tract. Nephrogenesis is complete by 34–36 weeks post-conception, in or ex utero. Prenatal and neonatal GFR is much lower than adult; adult GFR is reached by about 2 years, and renal growth continues past puberty. Tubular maturation (including sodium regulation) continues for weeks to months; sodium balance is a key neonatal function; limited potassium excretion gives higher serum potassium. CAKUT is the commonest cause of ESRD in children.

q: Which statement about defining interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) is FALSE?
o: Bladder-related pain is the core symptom
NIDDK criteria were made for research
Symptoms must last over six weeks
e: IC/BPS: an unpleasant sensation (pain, pressure, discomfort) perceived to relate to the bladder, with LUTS for more than 6 weeks, without infection or other cause; a diagnosis of exclusion with no specific test. Pain usually rises with filling and drives frequency; urgency (often misread by patients) and hydrodistention findings are not needed. NIDDK criteria ensure homogeneous research cohorts: 90% of experts agreed those patients had IC, but 60% of clinically diagnosed patients failed the criteria (high specificity, low sensitivity). Glomerulations lack sensitivity and specificity; they occur after radiation, with cancer, toxins, chemotherapy, dialysis or a defunctioned bladder, and mean nothing in an asymptomatic patient.

q: A boy has haematuria and hypertension 2 weeks after pharyngitis. The expected complement pattern is:
e: Post-infectious GN (and C3 glomerulopathy): low C3, normal C4. Lupus nephritis and MPGN: both low. ANCA-associated GN: normal complement. Confirm post-streptococcal disease with raised ASO titre.

q: Which statement about ED epidemiology is FALSE?
o: ED and CVD share a two-way risk link
Passive smoking has no link with ED
ED prevalence is about 20% of adult men
e: ED affects about 20% of adult men and rises with age. Predictors: older age, lower education, diabetes, cardiovascular disease (hypertension, stroke), active and passive smoke exposure, overweight. The ED–cardiovascular risk relationship is bidirectional; men with ED are 45% more likely to have a cardiac event within 5 years. Every ED patient carries some cardiovascular risk: basic medical assessment, health monitoring and lifestyle change (activity, weight) for all.

q: Which statement about staghorn and complex renal stones is FALSE?
o: Struvite stones must be fully cleared
Bladder urine best predicts PNL sepsis
Bacteria may hide deep inside stones
e: The best predictor of post-PNL urosepsis is stone or renal pelvic urine culture. Untreated staghorns: 10-year mortality 28% vs 7.2% with surgery; recurrent UTI, urosepsis and progressive loss of renal function. Struvite must be removed completely because bacteria in the stone keep urea-splitting bacteriuria going. Combined therapy for staghorns is primarily percutaneous, with SWL only as an adjunct to limit tracts. Cystinuric patients more often have reduced renal function.

q: A healthy 8-year-old has microscopic haematuria on a school screen. The first step is:
o: Renal biopsy to find the cause
e: Fewer than 25% persist on repeat testing. Persistent MH: screen renal function, ultrasound, urinary calcium and infection.

q: Which statement about adrenal anatomy is FALSE?
o: Both adrenals lie close to the diaphragmatic crus
The adrenals lie within Gerota fascia
Each gland gets inferior phrenic, aortic and renal branches
The right adrenal lies lower than the left
e: The right kidney lies lower than the left, but the right adrenal lies higher than the left. Both are near the diaphragmatic crus; the left touches the medial upper pole of the left kidney, with splenic vessels and pancreas anterior, aorta medial and psoas posterior. Arteries: superior (inferior phrenic), middle (aorta), inferior (renal), each splitting into 10–50 small arteries. The right adrenal vein is short and enters the IVC posterolaterally. The adrenals lie inside Gerota fascia.

q: Which statement about bladder filling is FALSE?
o: More collagen in the wall lowers compliance
Fibrotic low compliance responds to drugs
Normal filling barely raises bladder pressure
e: Normal physiological filling causes an almost imperceptible pressure rise: high compliance (ΔV/ΔP) from elastic and viscoelastic properties. Elasticity: stretch without tension; viscoelasticity: tension rises then decays (stress relaxation) when filling slows. Stroma (collagen, elastin) and a relaxed detrusor set passive properties; more collagen (injury, inflammation, obstruction, decentralisation) lowers compliance, and this is unresponsive to drugs, distention or nerve section: augmentation cystoplasty is usually needed.

q: The commonest cause of renal graft loss in children is:
e: Acute cellular rejection is common (first year <10% living donor, ~15% deceased donor) but usually responds to treatment; anastomotic failure is very rare; recurrent obstruction is usually manageable; antibody-mediated rejection is increasingly recognised.

q: Which statement about prostate and accessory gland development is FALSE?
o: Females form a prostate if androgens are high
Prostate development is driven by DHT
The prostate arises from the wolffian duct
e: Sex accessory tissues: prostate, seminal vesicles, ampullae, bulbourethral glands (not the tunica albuginea). Wolffian ducts form seminal vesicles, epididymis, vas, ampulla and ejaculatory duct under fetal testosterone, not DHT. The prostate arises from the urogenital sinus in the third month, driven mainly by DHT; with high enough androgens at the right time, even female embryos form a prostate; a functional androgen receptor in the mesenchyme is required. Estrogens are not needed: ER-α and ER-β knockout mice have normal prostates.

q: Which statement about haematuria in children is FALSE?
o: Heme-positive dipstick, no RBCs: think myoglobin
Isolated MH needs CT and cystoscopy
Most MH resolves within a year
e: Isolated microscopic haematuria (MH) occurs in about 1% of school-age children; on repeat testing under 25% persist; most resolve within a year. First step: repeat urinalysis in about 2 weeks; if persistent, screen renal function, structure (ultrasound), urinary calcium and infection. Gross haematuria with a heme-positive dipstick but no RBCs suggests haemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria.

q: 2,8-dihydroxyadenine stones in a child point to:
e: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT) deficiency is autosomal recessive. Alanine:glyoxylate aminotransferase (AGT) deficiency causes primary hyperoxaluria; secondary hyperoxaluria follows high oxalate or vitamin C intake or short gut. Cystinuria impairs reabsorption of cystine, ornithine, arginine and lysine.

q: Which statement about the Hunner lesion (HL) is FALSE?
o: Trigonal lesions should raise CIS concern
HL responds to fulguration or steroid
It is seen in over half of patients
Patients with HL tend to be older ones
e: HL (formerly Hunner ulcer) is pathognomonic of 'classic' IC, found in a minority (<30%); usually easy to see at office cystoscopy (distension beyond capacity or narrow-band imaging may help). Mounting evidence: BPS without HL is a distinct syndrome. HL patients are older, have fewer comorbidities and respond to bladder-centred therapy: fulguration and/or steroid injection. Clinical presentation otherwise does not reliably differ. HLs are supratrigonal; a trigonal lesion suggests CIS. Histology: dense, often panmural lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate; biopsy excludes CIS. Haematuria or pyuria do not predict HL; do office cystoscopy if HL suspected or empiric therapy fails.

q: Which stone type is most resistant to shock wave lithotripsy (SWL)?
e: Cystine and brushite are most resistant, then calcium oxalate monohydrate; then hydroxyapatite, struvite, calcium oxalate dihydrate and uric acid. SWL success falls linearly with Hounsfield density. Poor clearance after SWL: large stones, lower pole or obstructed segments, very hard stones and obesity. SWL causes acute (mainly vascular) renal injury in most patients.

q: Which feature points to an organic cause of ED?
e: Organic ED: gradual onset, incremental progression, global dysfunction and poor or absent morning erections. Shared decision making: the patient or couple chooses after discussing all options. Questionnaires document presence, subjective severity and treatment response, not cause or objective severity. IIEF domains: erectile function, orgasmic function, desire, intercourse satisfaction, overall satisfaction. Nocturnal tumescence does not necessarily mean erections adequate for intercourse.

q: Which statement about the prostate and seminal vesicles is FALSE?
o: Basal cells belong to the prostatic stroma
The seminal vesicles rarely get diseased
Stroma includes smooth muscle and fibroblasts
e: Two compartments: epithelium (basal, intermediate and neuroendocrine cells) and stroma (connective tissue, smooth muscle, fibroblasts). The prostate has a rich autonomic nerve plexus; of α1 subtypes (α1A, α1B, α1D), α1A is linked to contraction. The seminal vesicles are extremely resistant to disease.

q: Which cell is thought to play a central (though not primary) role in many IC/BPS patients?
e: Mast cells lie near vessels, lymphatics, nerves and detrusor; IC/BPS has neural, immune and endocrine components. Proposed local mechanisms: leaky epithelium, mast cell activation, neurogenic inflammation; widespread comorbid pain suggests global mechanisms in most.

q: Which statement about proteinuria in children is FALSE?
o: Normal UPC is under 0.2 mg/mg after infancy
A UPC of 0.5 mg/mg is nephrotic range
Fever and exercise increase urine protein
e: Urine normally contains protein, especially with fever and exercise; transient proteinuria accounts for >75% of isolated proteinuria. Normal UPC: <0.2 mg/mg in older children (higher in newborns); book: >1.0 is abnormal; >2.0 is nephrotic range. 24-hour protein: <200 mg in adolescents/adults, <4 mg/m²/h in young children. With systemic or glomerular features test C3, C4 and ANA.

q: Following the book, which pairing of renal stone and first-line treatment is FALSE?
o: Under 1 cm stone: SWL or ureteroscopy
e: Stone burden is the single most important factor. Book: <1 cm SWL or ureteroscopy; 1–2 cm (not lower pole) SWL or PNL; >2 cm PNL. Lower pole 10–25 mm (Lower Pole Study Group): stone-free 40% ureteroscopy vs 76% PNL; lower pole clearance is poorer for unclear reasons. Calyceal diverticular stones: PNL with fulguration gives the best stone- and symptom-free rate. Most untreated calyceal stones grow and cause pain or infection. Update: EAU accepts flexible ureteroscopy (RIRS) for 1–2 cm stones and PNL for >2 cm.

q: A woman with IC/BPS has high-tone pelvic floor dysfunction and obstructive voiding symptoms. Which therapy needs particular caution?
e: Botulinum toxin A (off-label) and SNM are book fourth-line options; retention is rare but caution is needed with obstructive voiding. Examination may show pelvic floor hypertonicity and tender points.

q: Which statement about urine storage is FALSE?
o: Striated sphincter activity rises with filling
Abdominal pressure is sent to the urethra
e: Spinal sympathetic reflexes facilitate filling/storage: sympathetic modulation of cholinergic ganglionic transmission inhibits the bladder, α-adrenergic stimulation tightens the smooth sphincter, β stimulation relaxes the bladder body. Guarding reflex: rising pudendal efferent activity and striated sphincter EMG during filling. Pelvic nerve outflow is sacral, but the micturition reflex is organised in the pontine-mesencephalic brainstem. Abdominal pressure is transmitted to the proximal urethra (and mid-urethra in women). Micturition has two phases: filling/storage and emptying/voiding.

q: Which statement about the course of IC/BPS is FALSE?
o: Prodromal symptoms may predate it by decades
Childhood onset is common in IC/BPS
Female relatives have 17 times the risk
Flares commonly follow diet or intercourse
e: Childhood presentation is extremely rare; average onset is 40 years. Presentation is subacute, often first treated as OAB or cystitis; prodromal LUTS or pelvic pain often date back decades. The disease is chronic, waxing and waning; remissions are common; flares (usually days) follow diet and physical activity such as sex or exercise. Adult female first-degree relatives have 17-fold prevalence. About 3 million women and 2 million men in the USA have symptoms (clinic ratio 5:1); prevalence has risen with looser definitions.

q: Which finding makes an IC/BPS patient a poor candidate for supratrigonal cystectomy and augmentation?
e: About 30% need self-catheterisation after augmentation, so urethral pain predicts a poor result. Fat stranding reflects panmural inflammation and does not matter. HL with a small, poorly compliant bladder predicts the best outcome; bowel segments may still become painful or contract.

q: Which statement about childhood nephrotic syndrome is FALSE?
o: Minimal change disease is the commonest cause
e: Minimal change disease is commonest; corticosteroids induce remission in the vast majority. FSGS is seen in most steroid-resistant children and becomes commoner in late childhood and adolescence; membranous and mesangial proliferative disease are less frequent. Congenital nephrotic syndrome presents before 3 months.

q: Which statement about specialised ED testing is FALSE?
o: Peak systolic velocity 30 cm/s is normal
e: Specialised testing improves accuracy but is not required before treatment; best used by specialists in complex presentations. Duplex ultrasound with intracavernosal injection (plus stimulation) gives a functional erection and assesses the whole penis from crura to tip. Peak systolic velocity <25 cm/s suggests arterial insufficiency; >35 cm/s is normal (25–35 is borderline). Angiography of iliac, internal pudendal and penile arteries is needed before penile revascularisation.

q: Which statement about opioids in IC/BPS is TRUE?
o: They should never be used in IC/BPS
They have a fixed analgesic ceiling
e: Opioids have no therapeutic ceiling (dose limited by side effects), cause constipation and sedation, and can help a subset with severe disease under 'universal precautions'.

q: Which statement about the adrenal gland is FALSE?
o: With renal agenesis the adrenal is present
The cortex is about 90% of gland mass
Zona fasciculata is 80% of the cortex
e: With renal ectopia or agenesis the adrenal is usually in its normal position. Cortex ≈90% of mass: glomerulosa (outer, ~15%, aldosterone), fasciculata (middle, ~80%, glucocorticoids), reticularis (inner, 5–7%, sex steroids). Reticularis androgens are regulated by ACTH, not LH. Adrenal rests lie near the coeliac axis and along the path of gonadal descent; in congenital adrenal hyperplasia cord rests may become large.

q: Which statement about ureteral stones is FALSE?
o: Most stones under 5 mm pass on their own
Distal stones pass more often than proximal
Tamsulosin is the preferred MET drug
e: Passage depends on size, location and side (smaller, distal and right-sided stones pass more), and on duration of symptoms and degree of hydronephrosis, not composition. Most stones <5 mm pass: expectant management. Alpha blockers increase passage; tamsulosin is preferred for efficacy and side effects. Update: SUSPEND (2015) showed no overall benefit, but later meta-analyses support MET for distal stones >5 mm; AUA recommends offering it for distal stones ≤10 mm. Distal ureteral stones: ureteroscopy stone-free 91% (AUA/EAU), better than SWL. For proximal stones with SWL, in situ treatment equals push-back.

q: Which statement about conditions linked with IC/BPS is FALSE?
o: Most patients have pain beyond the pelvis
Abuse history is a reported risk factor
e: Fibromyalgia, irritable bowel, chronic fatigue and atopic allergy are overrepresented (studied by the MAPP network). MAPP found two phenotypes: pelvic pain only and 'pelvic pain and beyond' (>75%), suggesting central pain. High-tone pelvic floor dysfunction: 70–94%. Overlapping disorders (pelvic floor, OAB, vulvodynia, IBS) need a multidisciplinary approach; missing them is a common cause of poor outcome. Abuse is a risk factor (Michigan: 37% of patients vs 22% of controls; abused patients have more pain, fewer voiding symptoms); be sensitive but do not assume. Sexual dysfunction strongly affects female quality of life. Cross-sensitisation between bowel and bladder may sustain pain.

q: Which statement about androgens is FALSE?
o: Most bound testosterone is on SHBG
Under 1% of testosterone comes from DHEA
e: Testosterone is synthesised from pregnenolone in Leydig cells by reversible steps; its reduction to DHT (5α-reductase) or aromatisation to estrogen is irreversible. Testosterone is a prohormone converted within the prostate to DHT. Less than 1% of plasma testosterone derives from DHEA; adrenal androgens have a minor role in prostate growth. Most protein-bound testosterone is on SHBG. Type 2 5α-reductase dominates in the prostate and is mutated in 5α-reductase deficiency.

q: The O'Leary-Sant symptom and problem indices are mainly used to:
e: Like the AUA symptom score for BPH, they grade severity and track progression, regression and treatment response; they are not diagnostic.

q: Which statement about childhood glomerulonephritis is FALSE?
o: ANCA vasculitis gives low C3 and C4
CT has no role in initial GN work-up
Post-infectious GN shows low C3, normal C4
e: Hypertension with gross haematuria after pharyngitis suggests post-streptococcal GN: urine sediment (cellular casts), renal function, electrolytes, ASO and C3; CT has no role. Complement: low C3 and C4 in lupus and MPGN; low C3, normal C4 in post-infectious GN and C3GN; normal in ANCA-associated GN (rare, older children, fever). Henoch-Schönlein purpura: purpura on legs/buttocks, abdominal pain, arthritis, nephritis. HUS follows bloody diarrhoea and is a common cause of severe AKI in previously well young children. IgA nephropathy is the commonest primary GN worldwide.

q: Which statement about neurogenic voiding dysfunction is FALSE?
o: Smooth dyssynergia goes with autonomic dysreflexia
e: Involuntary contractions occur mostly with suprasacral disease/injury, but also with ageing, inflammation, outlet obstruction, SUI or idiopathically. Stroke: urgency, frequency, urgency incontinence; detrusor overactivity with normal sensation and synergic sphincters (failure to store because of the bladder); ICS storage: overactive neurogenic detrusor, normal sensation, low capacity, normal compliance and closure; voiding normal. ICS 2002 replaced hyperreflexia/instability with neurogenic/idiopathic detrusor overactivity. Striated sphincter dyssynergia is commonest after complete suprasacral cord injury after spinal shock; smooth sphincter dyssynergia classically in autonomic hyperreflexia with DO and striated dyssynergia.

q: The main value of cystoscopy with hydrodistension under anaesthesia in IC/BPS is to:
e: It is not part of the standard diagnostic work-up; its main value is diagnosing HL, which responds well to resection or fulguration. 30–50% get short-term relief; ~30% flare briefly; anaesthetic capacity <200 mL is a poor prognostic sign.

q: Which statement about investigations in IC/BPS is FALSE?
o: The KCl test reliably confirms IC/BPS
e: Up to 25% of NIDDK-positive patients have a negative potassium chloride (KCl) test; it is positive in radiation cystitis, UTI, nonbacterial prostatitis and pelvic pain, uncomfortable and does not guide therapy. Cystometry: normal except reduced capacity and hypersensitivity; pain on filling reproducing symptoms is suggestive; compliance normal. Detrusor overactivity in ~15% is insignificant and does not exclude IC. No histology is pathognomonic; inflammation in 24–76%; biopsy excludes other disease. Symptom indices (O'Leary-Sant) monitor severity, not diagnose. Urine antiproliferative factor (APF) inhibits urothelial proliferation and is the best marker studied.

q: Which statement about percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PNL) is FALSE?
o: Non-contrast CT detects residual stones well
e: 43% of patients with residual fragments later had a symptomatic episode or needed intervention. Non-contrast CT had 100% sensitivity versus flexible nephroscopy (the traditional gold standard). Absolute contraindications: uncorrected coagulopathy and active untreated UTI. Physiological irrigant prevents dilutional hyponatraemia if extravasation occurs. Matrix stones (gelatinous): PNL best; SWL ineffective; ureteroscopy hampered by volume.

q: Which is a contraindication to intracavernosal injection therapy?
e: Contraindications: psychological instability, priapism history or risk, severe coagulopathy, unstable cardiovascular disease, reduced dexterity and MAO inhibitor use.

q: Which statement about testosterone testing in ED is FALSE?
o: Draw blood for it between 7 and 11 AM
Bioavailable T is free plus SHBG T
e: Testosterone circulates free, albumin-bound and SHBG-bound; bioavailable = free + albumin-bound. Factors raising SHBG lower bioavailable testosterone. Production is circadian with a morning peak: sample between 7 and 11 AM. The aim of testosterone therapy is symptomatic improvement, usually titrated to normal levels. Endocrine causes of ED: hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism, diabetes.

q: Which statement about the androgen receptor (AR) is FALSE?
o: Longer CAG repeats make the AR more active
Ligand binding releases AR from chaperones
AR dimers bind response elements head to head
e: After binding ligand, AR leaves its chaperonins, dimerises and enters the nucleus via a nuclear localisation motif (Ran-dependent, ATP-dependent active transport); it shuttles back to the cytoplasm; the nuclear matrix is the main nuclear binding target for androgen and estrogen receptors. Shorter poly-CAG repeats mean a more active AR; longer means less. Crystallography shows dimers bind head to head whether the response element is a direct or inverted repeat.

q: The best predictor of urosepsis after PNL is:
o: Stone or renal pelvic urine culture
e: Bacteria reside deep in stones; bladder urine may be sterile while pelvic urine or stone is infected.

q: An infant fails to thrive with a normal anion gap acidosis, very low bicarbonate and nephrocalcinosis. Diagnosis:
e: Hyperchloraemic (normal anion gap) metabolic acidosis is the hallmark of RTA. Distal RTA: very low bicarbonate, hypokalaemia, hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis. Proximal RTA/Fanconi: bicarbonate usually 12–14 mEq/L with hypophosphataemia, low-grade proteinuria and glycosuria. Hyperkalaemic RTA is type 4. Bartter syndrome is defined by hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; Dent disease does not cause RTA.

q: Which statement about the differential diagnosis of IC/BPS is FALSE?
o: Bladder CIS can be misdiagnosed as IC
Some CPPS category III men meet IC criteria
Bacterial prostatitis is a form of IC/BPS
e: Ketamine cystitis mimics IC/BPS and can involve the upper tracts: ask about recreational drugs, especially in the young. NIH type I (acute) and II (chronic bacterial) prostatitis have known causes and no relationship to IC/BPS; some men with category III CPPS meet IC criteria. Men with irritative symptoms and pelvic pain: evaluate for IC/BPS vs CIS, outlet obstruction and bacterial prostatitis; many have had needless bladder neck surgery. Bladder cancer can be misdiagnosed as IC; most reports show no link to later cancer (Mayo cases were misdiagnosis; a Taiwanese study found RR 2.95). Other pelvic pain syndromes: vulvodynia, orchialgia, perineal, penile and rectal pain.

q: Which statement about classification of voiding dysfunction is FALSE?
o: Spasticity below the lesion implies a UMN lesion
A reflex bladder follows complete cord injury
Bors-Comarr unbalanced UMN means PVR over 10%
Lapides split atonic bladders into two types
e: Lapides modified McLellan by splitting 'atonic' into sensory and motor neurogenic bladder; uninhibited neurogenic bladder was ascribed to corticoregulatory tract injury. Reflex neurogenic bladder: after spinal shock, complete interruption between sacral cord and brainstem (trauma, transverse myelitis): no sensation, no voluntary voiding, low-volume DO incontinence, striated dyssynergia (= complete UMN in Bors-Comarr). Bors-Comarr (neurological patients only): lesion level, completeness, balance; unbalanced = residual >20% of capacity for UMN, >10% for LMN. Skeletal spasticity below the lesion implies UMN (DO); flaccidity implies LMN (areflexia).

q: Which statement about ED pharmacotherapy is FALSE?
o: Nitrates absolutely bar PDE5 inhibitor use
e: Erection needs nitric oxide from nerves and endothelium; cGMP and cAMP relax corporal smooth muscle. Any nitrate absolutely contraindicates PDE5 inhibitors. Injectables: prostaglandin E1, papaverine, phentolamine. Alprostadil: less prolonged erection, systemic effects and fibrosis; but more painful erection, higher cost, short half-life once reconstituted. Injection contraindications: psychological instability, priapism risk, severe coagulopathy, unstable cardiovascular disease, poor dexterity, MAO inhibitors. Penile rehabilitation with PDE5 inhibitors after RP has not proved efficacious.

q: For 10–25 mm lower pole stones, stone-free rates at 3 months for PNL versus ureteroscopy (Lower Pole Study Group) were:
e: PNL was significantly better than ureteroscopy for lower pole stones of this size.

q: Which statement about seminal fluid is FALSE?
o: Fructose comes from the seminal vesicles
Seminal vesicles give most semen volume
e: Seminal vesicles: prostaglandins, fructose (absent with congenital absence of the vesicles), semenogelin, and most of the volume. Prostate: citrate, zinc, spermine, choline. PSA is a serine protease that degrades semenogelin (which coagulates semen). Complexed PSA is irreversibly bound to α1-antichymotrypsin and α2-macroglobulin; rises in hK2, pro-PSA and bound PSA are associated with cancer. Prostatic fluid is more acidic than serum.

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: ARPKD is due to polycystin-1 mutations
MCDK has urologic anomalies in up to 25%
Ultrasound is first imaging for renal colic
Calcium stones are commonest in children
e: ARPKD: PKHD1 gene, with hepatic fibrosis; ADPKD: PKD1 (polycystin-1) or PKD2; childhood ultrasound in ADPKD ranges from normal to severe cysts. MCDK: associated anomalies in up to 25% (hypoplasia/dysplasia, VUR, UPJ obstruction). Paediatric urolithiasis is underdiagnosed (often asymptomatic); calcium stones most prevalent; ultrasound is the first study for colic (CT adds radiation); give analgesia before drainage.

q: With complete ureteral obstruction, irreversible loss of renal function begins after about:
e: Irreversible loss starts after about 2 weeks and total unit loss can occur by 6 weeks; do not leave a significant obstruction beyond 2–4 weeks.

q: Which statement about stone treatment in special situations is FALSE?
o: Routine stenting before SWL aids breakup
SWL suits small diverticular stones that drain
e: AUA panel: routine stenting before SWL does not improve fragmentation; stents are for pain, obstruction, poorly visualised stones and are mandatory with an obstructed solitary kidney. If anticoagulation cannot stop, ureteroscopy with holmium laser is preferred (successful even with incompletely corrected coagulopathy). Morbid obesity: retrograde intrarenal surgery when stone burden is modest. SWL for small (<1.5 cm) stones with good drainage; otherwise PNL first.

q: Which statement about initial IC/BPS treatment is FALSE?
o: Long-term antibiotics are a core therapy
Patient education is the most important step
e: Antibiotics have no role and infection is not causative (one empiric doxycycline trial is reasonable if never tried). Initial care: education (chronic, waxing-waning, remissions; uninformed patients are easy prey), diet changes, non-prescription analgesics, pelvic floor relaxation. Elimination diets identify food/drink sensitivities. Catastrophising increases pain and responds to cognitive behavioural therapy. Start conservatively and escalate for poor control, or start aggressively when symptoms are severe.

q: The right adrenal vein:
o: Is long and enters the IVC anteriorly
Joins the right inferior phrenic vein first
Drains into the right renal vein usually
Is short, entering the IVC posterolaterally
e: The short right adrenal vein is a classic source of bleeding at right adrenalectomy. (The left adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein.) Each gland receives superior (inferior phrenic), middle (aortic) and inferior (renal) arteries.

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Urgency is the key symptom of OAB
Effort leakage in women implies some ISD
e: ICS: OAB is urgency, with or without urgency incontinence, usually with frequency and nocturia; about one-third have incontinence. Detrusor overactivity is a urodynamic finding that may or may not accompany urgency. Female outlet-related incontinence combines loss of support (hypermobility) and ISD; effort incontinence always involves some ISD. Male outlet incontinence (usually after prostatectomy) is essentially ISD. Two sphincters: smooth (bladder neck/proximal urethra, involuntary) and striated (intramural rhabdosphincter plus external levator part, voluntary). Hammock hypothesis: the ventral urethra is compressed against a fixed fascial dorsal support. Inflammation increases afferent input and pain hypersensitivity.

q: Which statement about hypertension in children is FALSE?
o: White coat hypertension affects up to 25%
One raised office reading confirms it
Lifestyle change is first for primary HT
Obesity drives the rise in prevalence
e: Elevated office BP should be repeated (e.g., 1–2 weeks) to confirm; ambulatory monitoring is recommended where available. If confirmed: metabolic panel, lipids, echocardiography and renal ultrasound; angiography and renal vein renins for severe or resistant cases. Up to a quarter have white coat hypertension. Rising prevalence tracks obesity. Primary hypertension without end-organ damage: lifestyle changes first (AAP 2017 guideline).

q: In the Bors-Comarr system, an LMN lesion is 'unbalanced' when residual urine exceeds:
e: Unbalanced: residual >20% of capacity with a UMN lesion, >10% with an LMN lesion; this was meant to imply sphincter dyssynergia.

q: Which statement about IC/BPS drug therapy is FALSE?
o: Pentosan targets the urothelial GAG layer
Pentosan and DMSO are the FDA-approved drugs
Pentosan has been linked to maculopathy
e: Pentosan polysulfate (oral heparin analogue) aims to repair the glycosaminoglycan (GAG) layer; chronic use is linked to pigmentary maculopathy (AUA 2022 advises eye examinations). Pentosan (oral) and DMSO (intravesical) are the only FDA-approved drugs. Amitriptyline (not approved) helps via antihistamine, sedative and neuropathic pain effects at doses below antidepressant doses; anticholinergic effects may worsen constipation or voiding. Intravesical agents have limited success in centralised pain; dosing and maintenance are poorly studied. Book: none of the agents listed in its question had positive double-blind placebo-controlled trials. In a bladder-centric patient, untreated vestibulodynia or pelvic floor pain hides the benefit of intravesical therapy.

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Vacuum devices engorge the glans too
Internal pudendal stenosis is the usual target
Ideal revascularisation candidate had perineal trauma
e: Penile revascularisation is reserved for: perineal/pelvic trauma, age <55, nondiabetic, nonsmoker, no venous leak and a documented internal pudendal artery stenosis on angiography. Vacuum erection devices engorge the whole penis including the glans, helping glanular insufficiency; also suggested to preserve elasticity after priapism, prosthesis removal or Peyronie surgery.

q: Which statement about adrenal imaging is FALSE?
o: Ultrasound separates solid from cystic masses
CT is the most used adrenal imaging test
Under 10 HU on plain CT suggests benign tissue
CT and MRI give functional information
e: CT is the most widely used modality; ultrasound distinguishes solid from cystic masses; MRI (T1/T2, chemical shift) helps characterise masses. CT and MRI give morphology only, no functional data. Book: normal adrenal tissue is ≤10 HU on non-contrast CT. Note: in practice ≤10 HU is the threshold diagnosing a lipid-rich benign adenoma in an adrenal mass.

q: Which statement about paediatric AKI and kidney failure is FALSE?
o: FeNa over 1% points to prerenal AKI
Peritoneal dialysis is first under 20 kg
CRRT is standard in critically ill children
Hospitalised children with AKI have 15× mortality
e: Prerenal AKI (dehydration from vomiting/diarrhoea): urine sodium <25 mEq/L or FeNa <1%; treat promptly with isotonic fluids. Intrinsic disease (valves, interstitial nephritis, UTI) shows FeNa >1%. AKI in hospitalised children carries nearly 15-fold mortality. CRRT is standard, correcting fluid and electrolytes slowly. Peritoneal dialysis is the commonest initial modality under 9 years and 20 kg.

q: The dominant 5α-reductase isoform in the prostate is:
e: Type 2 is mutated in 5α-reductase deficiency, in which prostatic development is severely impaired.

q: Which statement about refractory IC/BPS is FALSE?
o: Capacity under 200 mL under anaesthesia is poor
Opioids can help a subset with severe pain
e: Hydrodistension under anaesthesia: mainly diagnoses HL; short-term relief in 30–50%, brief flare in ~30%; capacity <200 mL is a poor sign; a low anaesthetic capacity marks a bladder-centric phenotype (higher scores, less depression/IBS); glomerulations are unnecessary. Opioids (no ceiling, dependence, constipation, sedation) can help some severe cases under universal precautions. Book: SNM and botulinum toxin are fourth-line; caution with toxin when voiding is obstructive (high-tone pelvic floor). Update: AUA 2022 no longer ranks therapies in lines. Diversion or cystectomy cannot guarantee pain relief; best results with HL and a small, poorly compliant bladder; bowel segments may become painful or contract; urethral pain is a poor sign for augmentation (≈30% need CISC); perivesical fat stranding on CT does not matter.

q: Which statement about stones and obstruction is FALSE?
o: Obstructing stones shouldn't persist beyond 2–4 weeks
Pregnant women admitted for colic deliver early more often
Indinavir and triamterene can form stones
e: Pregnancy causes absorptive hypercalciuria and mild hyperuricosuria, offset by more citrate, magnesium and urine output; admission for colic raises preterm delivery risk. Complete obstruction: irreversible loss after about 2 weeks, total loss by up to 6 weeks; no clear human threshold, worse with vascular disease, low reserve, malnutrition or diabetes: do not leave a significant obstruction beyond 2–4 weeks. Drug stones: ephedrine, indinavir, triamterene, magnesium trisilicate, ciprofloxacin, sulfa drugs.

q: Besides prostate cancer, serum acid phosphatase may be raised in:
e: Acid phosphatase is also produced in bone, so it may rise in Paget disease, osteoporosis and bone metastases.

q: Which statement about prostate pharmacology and markers is FALSE?
o: Acid phosphatase rises in Paget disease of bone
Most antibiotics reach high prostatic levels
e: Few drugs reach prostatic fluid levels near serum: exceptions are erythromycin, oleandomycin, sulfonamides, tetracycline, clindamycin, trimethoprim and fluoroquinolones. Testosterone half-life 10–20 min, so bilateral orchiectomy gives castration within 1–2 h (book). Measure testosterone in the morning (diurnal variation). Prostatic acid phosphatase may rise in prostate cancer but also comes from bone (Paget disease, osteoporosis, metastases).

q: Which statement about paediatric CKD and transplantation is FALSE?
o: Living-donor rejection is under 10% in year one
CKD growth failure is true GH deficiency
Recombinant GH is needed in most children
Chronic allograft nephropathy is the main loss
e: CKD growth failure stems from abnormal growth hormone activity, not deficiency, plus malnutrition, anaemia (mainly erythropoietin deficiency), acidosis and failed 1α-hydroxylation of vitamin D; nutrition alone is often insufficient, so recombinant GH is used in most. Causes of CKD differ from adults and by age; decline is nonlinear (faster late). Transplantation improves growth, neurocognition and QoL. First-year acute rejection: <10% living donor, ~15% deceased donor; usually responsive. Chronic allograft nephropathy is the commonest cause of graft loss; antibody-mediated rejection increasingly recognised. Hyperoxaluria may be primary (AGT deficiency) or secondary (diet, vitamin C, short gut); APRT deficiency causes 2,8-dihydroxyadenine stones; cystinuria impairs reabsorption of cystine, ornithine, arginine, lysine.

q: Which change is associated with prostate cancer?
o: A fall in human kallikrein 2 level
Rises in hK2, pro-PSA and bound PSA
e: Complexed PSA is irreversibly bound to α1-antichymotrypsin and α2-macroglobulin. Cancer is associated with more hK2, pro-PSA and bound PSA (so a lower free fraction).
